Within me dwelt a small donkey. I placed no faith in magic, yet the donkey was utterly enchanted by it—psychics, illusionists, arthritics who could foretell the rainfall. That was the year I struggled to walk. I overthought every step and could never quite find the rhythm. So the donkey taught me anew. "This foot. Yes, then the other. And swing your arms as though marching to trial to be acquitted of a crime you have most assuredly committed."

Then came the trouble sleeping, for I had to crank the generator in my chest so incessantly. Perceiving how overworked I had become, the donkey at last wrenched it free—it gleamed bright and new, like a silver dollar—and hurled it into a flock of birds, who were forced to fly a great distance to find safety. In that moment I understood that I was a large and dangerous man, harboring this donkey within me, and yet I felt wholly powerless.

One day, during a final lesson on breathing, the donkey inquired what sort of jeans I was wearing. "The somber ones," I replied.

"Poor child."

"So will you be staying on for a third year, donkey?"

"No. I believe I should be departing soon. I believe I shall go and await your arrival beside the crumpled river."

"Yes, I suppose you have many pressing matters to attend to. But perhaps one day I will come and join you—for a drink, or, it may be, for a brief nap."

# The Donkey Within

There is a donkey inside me. Not a metaphor I reach for lightly, but a presence I have come to know as intimately as my own pulse. Where I am skeptical, quick to dismiss the unexplainable, and suspicious of anything that cannot be measured or proven, the donkey is different. The donkey believes. It is fascinated by magic, drawn to the supernatural, forever leaning toward the mysteries I would rather turn away from. In this way, we are opposites sharing a single body—my doubt and its wonder, bound together whether I like it or not.

During one particular year, when my body seemed to fail me at every turn, it was the donkey who kept me alive. Patiently, without complaint, it taught me again the things I had forgotten how to do. It showed me how to walk, placing one foot ahead of the other as though I were a child learning for the first time. It taught me how to sleep when sleep would not come, and how to breathe when even that most basic act felt like labor. The donkey never grew frustrated with my slowness. It simply stayed, and instructed, and waited for me to relearn what my body had lost.

I remember the strangest of its acts most clearly. The donkey reached into my chest and removed something from within me—a small generator, round and bright, no larger than a silver dollar. Then it flung the thing away, casting it toward a flock of birds that had gathered nearby, searching for safety. Whatever that generator had been humming inside me, the donkey decided I no longer needed it, and let it go.

Because of the donkey, I have come to understand that I am a large and dangerous man. The creature within me carries a weight and a wildness that I cannot fully control, and I feel its capacity for harm as surely as I feel its tenderness. And yet, knowing this brings me no triumph—only a quiet sense of futility, as though all this strength amounts to something I cannot use or direct toward any purpose that matters.

In the end, the donkey told me it was leaving. It would go on ahead, it said, to wait for me beside a crumpled river. I understood what it meant. It would be there at the edge of things, patient as ever, holding its place until I finally arrived—not in this life, but in whatever comes after it. We would meet again, the donkey and I, in death.
outputs.L4:
**The Donkey Who Lived Inside Me**

There has always been a donkey living inside me, and he loves magic more than anything. I do not know how he arrived, or when, only that he was there before I understood the word *before*, folding coins into his ears and pulling scarves from the dark cavity behind my heart.

It was the donkey who taught me to walk.

I remember nothing of this, of course, but he has told me the story so many times that it has become a kind of memory. He stood behind my knees, he says, and whispered *left, now right, now left again,* until my legs learned the arithmetic of forward motion. When I stumbled, he caught me with his soft gray muzzle. When I wept, he performed a small trick—a flower from nowhere, a light behind his teeth—and I forgot that I had ever been afraid of the ground.

He taught me to sleep, too. On the long nights when the ceiling seemed to breathe and every shadow wore a face, the donkey would lie down in the meadow of my chest and hum. His song had no words, only the shape of grass bending, and I would close my eyes and follow him into the fields where nothing waited to hurt me. In the morning he would nudge me awake, delighted, as though waking were the greatest illusion of all—the reappearance of the whole disappeared world.

And he taught me to breathe. This was his simplest magic and his greatest. *In,* he said, and the air was a rabbit; *out,* he said, and the rabbit was gone. In, out. The rabbit, the emptiness. He made a rhythm of it, a card trick I performed a hundred thousand times a day without applause, without even noticing the wonder of it. That the body should insist on continuing. That the lungs should be so easily fooled into hope.

For years I thought he would stay forever. What is more permanent than the thing that lives inside you, closer than your own name?

But one evening—I could not tell you the season, only that the light had gone the color of old paper—the donkey came to the front of me and pressed his forehead to the inside of my ribs. His eyes were kind and enormous. He said he had one more trick to show me, and that it was the oldest trick, the one all the others had been rehearsals for.

"I am going," he said, "to await your arrival beside the crumpled river."

I asked him where that was. I asked him how I would find it. But a donkey who loves magic never explains the mechanism; that would spoil everything. He only told me that he would go on ahead, as he always had, one step in front of my faltering steps. That he would stand at the water and hum his wordless song. That when I finally came stumbling down to the bank—tired, unlearning at last how to walk, how to sleep, how to breathe—he would be there to catch me with his soft gray muzzle, the way he did when I was new to the world and afraid of falling.

Then he pulled the last scarf from the dark behind my heart, and it was the color of everything, and when it drifted down there was no donkey behind it. Only the empty meadow of my chest, still faintly warm, still faintly smelling of grass.

I breathe in. The rabbit appears. I breathe out. It is gone.

I am learning, slowly, that this too was something he taught me: how to hold the disappearing and call it living. And I walk on, left, now right, now left again, toward the river I have never seen, where someone patient and small is practicing the trick of my return.

# Inside the World of Psychics

Have you ever wondered what really goes on **inside** the mind of someone who claims to see beyond the ordinary? The world of **psychics** has fascinated humanity for centuries, drawing curious minds and skeptics alike into conversations about intuition, energy, and the unknown.

## What Lies Inside

Many people believe **that** every person carries a certain intuitive ability locked **inside** them. Psychics often describe their gift as an extension of this natural instinct—something everyone possesses but few fully develop. They claim **that** by quieting the noise of daily life and looking **inside**, one can access insights **that** aren't visible on the surface.

## The Appeal of Psychics

Why do so many turn to **psychics** in times of uncertainty? Some seek comfort after losing a loved one. Others hope **that** a reading will illuminate a difficult decision or reveal what the future holds. Whatever the reason, there's no denying **that** the practice fills an emotional need for connection and meaning.

## A Balanced Perspective

Critics argue **that** the claims made by **psychics** cannot be scientifically proven. Supporters counter **that** not everything valuable can be measured in a laboratory. The truth, perhaps, lives somewhere **inside** the space between belief and doubt.

Whether you're a devoted believer or a curious skeptic, one thing remains clear: the mystery **that** surrounds **psychics** continues to spark wonder about what truly exists **inside** the human experience.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a person who has a small donkey living inside them, teaching them how to walk, sleep, and breathe.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Donkey Inside

There is a donkey inside me the size of a thumb, and it has been teaching me how to be alive since before I knew I was.

*This is how you walk,* it says, and lifts one small hoof against the wall of my ribs. *You do not fall. You lean into falling and catch yourself with the next foot. All walking is falling that has agreed not to finish.* And I walk, tipping forward through the days, always about to hit the ground, always saved by the animal patience of my own two feet.

At night the donkey folds its legs beneath it the way donkeys do, tucking down into the warm hay of me. *This is how you sleep,* it whispers, breath smelling of thistle and old rain. *You put down the load you carried. You do not need to guard the road until morning. The road guards itself.* And I set my burdens by the door of my body, and the donkey keeps its dark eye half-open so I don't have to.

*Breathe,* it says, and I forget, and it says it again — *breathe* — nudging the bellows of my lungs with its soft gray nose. In, and the sky comes down the well of my throat. Out, and I give the sky back, unharmed. *You are only borrowing the air,* the donkey reminds me. *Every breath is a thing returned. This is why the dying exhale. They are simply finished being polite.*

Sometimes I feel it braying in my chest at things I cannot see — grief coming up the mountain, or joy, or the mailman. Sometimes it stops in the middle of my life and will not move, and no amount of pulling helps, and I have learned this too is a kind of wisdom: the stubbornness that knows a cliff is near before the eyes do.

I do not know how the donkey got inside me. I think perhaps we all have one, some small gray teacher patient as furniture, showing us the ancient work of staying. Showing us that the body is a country we did not choose and cannot leave, and that somewhere in its hills a little animal is always saying, gently, gently:

*here is how you live —*
*one falling step,*
*one folded night,*
*one borrowed breath*
*at a time.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of experimental flash fiction in the style of a fable, using strange metaphors and dreamlike logic, about an inner creature that departs.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Tenant of the Ribcage

For years a small animal lived behind my sternum, and I fed it what animals eat: unanswered letters, the blue hour before sleep, the particular weight of Sundays.

It was neither cat nor bird but something in between, stitched from both and from a third thing I have no word for. When I laughed too loudly it would flinch. When I lied it grew a new tooth.

One morning I woke to find it standing at the gate of my throat, holding a suitcase made of my own held breath.

"I am leaving," it said, in the voice of a door that has decided.

"But I built the whole house around you," I told it. "The rooms are your shape. The windows only open the way you like."

The creature set down its suitcase, which sighed. "That was the problem," it said. "You made a museum of me. Every day you dusted my edges and would not let me change. An animal that cannot change is only a picture of an animal."

I offered it the good grief, the aged kind I kept in the cellar. I offered it a river I had been saving. I offered to become smaller, so it might have more room.

But it had already begun to walk out through the front of me, and where it passed, the walls turned to weather.

"When you need me," it called back, growing translucent as a rumor, "do not look inward. I will be the thing tapping at other people's windows. I will be the animal in the animal you meet on the road."

Then it was gone, and my chest was a wide field at dusk, and—strange, strange—I did not collapse.

I simply stood there, ringing like a bell that has finally been emptied of its clapper, and discovered I could hold much more of the sky than I had ever guessed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a whimsical, absurdist monologue in which the narrator describes their relationship with a magical donkey that lives inside their body across three years.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Donkey Within: A Three-Year Chronicle

Let me be clear from the outset: I did not *ask* for a magical donkey to take up residence in my body. These things simply happen to a person, the way hiccups happen, or the way you suddenly remember an embarrassing thing you said in 2009 while trying to fall asleep.

**Year One** was, frankly, a nightmare of adjustment.

I first noticed him on a Tuesday—donkeys always arrive on Tuesdays, I'm told—when I bent down to tie my shoe and heard, quite distinctly, a soft *hee-haw* emanating from somewhere near my liver. "Hello?" I said to my own torso, which is not a sentence one plans to say. The donkey did not respond. Donkeys, I would learn, are terrible conversationalists but excellent listeners, which makes them ideal for people who enjoy monologuing at their organs.

He ate my worries. This was his one great gift. Every anxiety I produced, he'd chomp it down like an apple. Unfortunately, he produced *opinions* in return, and they came out through my kneecaps as a faint braying whenever I made a poor decision. He brayed a great deal that first year.

**Year Two** brought a fragile peace.

We reached an understanding, the donkey and I. I named him Bartholomew, because he refused all other names by kicking my ribs from the inside—a sensation not unlike being disagreed with by a sneeze. Bartholomew and I developed rituals. Each morning I would drink a glass of water, and he would gallop joyously through my bloodstream, which felt like being tickled by a rumor.

He grew wise that year, my internal donkey. When I could not decide whether to call an old friend, Bartholomew would stamp *once* for yes, *twice* for "you know very well what you did, and no." I began to trust him more than my own brain, which had, after all, never once eaten a single worry and had instead spent decades hoarding them like a dragon with excellent recall.

**Year Three** was the year of departure.

Magical donkeys, you see, do not stay forever. They are migratory in the way that courage is migratory—present exactly when required, and then off to some other frightened soul who needs a beast of burden lodged near their spleen.

I felt him leaving on an ordinary Thursday (they leave on Thursdays; the asymmetry is intentional and cruel). There was one final *hee-haw*, softer now, almost tender, echoing up through my chest and out through the crown of my head like a balloon released by a distracted child.

And then he was gone.

I am donkeyless now. I carry my own worries again, and they are heavy, and no one brays at me from my kneecaps when I text the wrong person at midnight. But sometimes—*sometimes*—when I bend down to tie my shoe, I swear I hear the distant thunder of tiny hooves, and I remember that once, for three impossible years, I was never alone inside my own skin.

Thank you, Bartholomew.

Wherever you are galloping now, I hope the worries are plentiful and sweet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic vignette blending magical realism and melancholy, featuring imagery like a silver dollar heart, somber jeans, and a crumpled river.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Small Currencies

The boy wore somber jeans the color of a Tuesday
that never quite arrives—
belt loops empty as promises,
pockets holding nothing but the echo
of coins he'd never spend.

In his chest, a silver dollar heart
ticked its slow oxidation,
tarnishing one heartbeat at a time.
He could feel it turning green
the way old love does,
the way a penny forgets its copper shine
beneath the tongue of years.

Down by the crumpled river—
that ribbon someone folded wrong
and tried to smooth back flat,
its water creased with memory—
he pressed his palm against the current
and watched his reflection wrinkle
like a photograph left in the rain.

*Here*, the river seemed to say,
*is where the drowned things dream.*

He offered up his silver dollar heart,
that ancient minted thing,
and the water took it gently,
the way grief takes everything gently
in the end.

It sank.
It caught the last coin of the sunlight.
And for one impossible moment
the whole crumpled river
smoothed itself smooth,
remembering how to be
a mirror
for a boy in somber jeans
who had, at last,
paid the fare
across.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a strange, lyrical short story about learning to live in your own body, narrated as a conversation with an internal donkey who eventually says goodbye.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Donkey in the Chest

The donkey arrived the year I stopped sleeping. I never asked how it fit inside me, between the ladder of ribs and the wet drum of the heart. It simply was there, the way weather is there.

*You're breathing wrong again,* it said the first time it spoke. Its voice was gray and patient, like fog learning to be a wall.

I told it I didn't know there was a right way.

*There isn't,* it said. *But there's a wrong one, and you've perfected it.*

---

We learned each other slowly, the donkey and I. It liked to speak in the early hours when the body was quietest, when I could feel the whole architecture of myself, every hinge and hollow.

*Put your feet on the floor,* it would say. *Feel the floor put itself back.*

I didn't understand at first. I thought a body was a thing you dragged behind you, a wet coat you couldn't take off. I thought I lived somewhere above it, in a small lit room behind the eyes, sending down instructions no one obeyed.

*You live everywhere,* the donkey said. *In the ankle. In the soft place behind the knee. You've been trying to fit your whole self into your skull. No wonder it aches.*

---

The donkey was not gentle, exactly. Donkeys aren't. It refused to carry what wasn't mine.

Once I tried to load it with an old shame, a heavy grinding stone I'd hauled since childhood.

*Not that,* it said, and stood very still. *That was never yours. Someone handed it to you when you were too small to say no.*

I said I didn't know how to set it down.

*Open your hands,* said the donkey. *That's all setting-down is. Hands remembering they can open.*

I opened my hands. The stone did not vanish. But it rolled a little way off, and sat in the grass, and became just a stone.

---

Years went like this. The donkey teaching me the country of myself, one small field at a time. *This is hunger,* it would say. *This is tiredness wearing hunger's mask. This is grief, and it lives in the throat, and it wants only to be let through, not kept.*

I grew less afraid of the dark rooms inside me. I learned that a body is not a sentence but a language, and I was slowly, clumsily, becoming fluent.

*You laughed today,* the donkey noted one evening. *With your whole belly. I felt it. Like rain on a tin roof.*

I hadn't noticed. That was the miracle of it—I had stopped narrating my own joy from a distance. I had simply *been there* for it, inside the animal warmth of an ordinary Tuesday.

---

Then one morning the donkey said, *I think I'll be going soon.*

Something in me lurched. I said I still needed it. I said I wasn't finished.

*You're never finished,* it said, not unkindly. *But you don't need me to translate anymore. You've learned the words. Listen—*

And I listened, and I heard it: my own heartbeat, no longer frightening. The tide of breath. The small conversations between muscle and bone that go on all day whether we attend to them or not. My body, speaking to itself in a language I finally, mostly, understood.

*See,* said the donkey. *You were always the one talking. I was only the echo you needed to believe it.*

---

It left the way weather leaves—no door, no ceremony, just a slow clearing. One day the gray patient voice was simply the sound of my own thoughts, indistinguishable, gathered home.

*Be good to the animal,* were its last words, or maybe mine. *It carried you here. It will carry you the rest of the way. Feed it. Rest it. Let it into the sun.*

I put my feet on the floor.

I felt the floor put itself back.

And I stayed—for once, entirely—inside the small warm house of myself, which no longer felt so small, and had never, it turned out, been anywhere but home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
